fetched_contents.text: Farm Environmental Enrichments Improve the Welfare of Layer Chicks and Pullets: A Comprehensive Review Abstract Simple Summary Layer industries that are still using cage housing systems should encourage the provision of appropriate farm enrichments, especially at an early stage. Farm environmental enrichments such as litter, sand, alfalfa bales, chick papers, pecking stones, pecking strings, perches, slopes, elevated platforms, aviaries and outdoor access reduce feather and skin damage, as well as abdominal fat content. Additionally, they promote the development of the brain and musculoskeletal systems and improve biological function, productivity and product quality with lifelong benefits for hens by continuously exposing them to free access to forage, dust baths and free locomotion. In this review, we summarize several common and effective methods of farm environmental enrichments, including different manipulable materials, structural equipment, and outdoor access, moreover, the competence of the farm staff is a requirement to achieve useful utilization of these farm environmental enrichments that aim to reduce stress and improve the welfare and productivity of layers. Proper farm environmental enrichments benefit the wellbeing of caged birds. Abstract Currently, cage housing is regarded as a global mainstream production system for laying hens. However, limited living space and confinement of birds in cages cause welfare and health problems, such as feather pecking, osteoporosis, obesity, and premature aging. Many studies have been conducted to alleviate layer welfare problems by providing farm environmental enrichments such as litter, sand, alfalfa bales, chick papers, pecking stones, pecking strings, perches, slopes, elevated platforms, aviaries and outdoor access with a trend towards complex enrichments. The provision of appropriate enrichments continuously attracts layers towards pecking, foraging, dust bathing, and locomotion, thereby giving lifelong benefits to laying hens. Hence, raising chicks and pullets under such conditions may reduce feather and skin damage, as well as accumulation of abdominal fat, and improve several biological features such as health, productivity, quality products, and docility of laying hens. Therefore, providing enrichment during the first few days of the layer’s life without any interruption is crucial. In addition, due to different farm conditions, environmental enrichment should be managed by well-trained farm staff. For example, in preventing feather pecking among the birds, litter materials for foraging are superior to dust bath materials or new items. However, a limited supply of litter creates competition and challenges among birds. Therefore, providing farm environmental enrichment for layers requires proper handling, especially in commercial layer farms. Hence, improving the welfare of chicks and pullets through optimizing on-farm environmental enrichments is essential for production systems practicing cage housing. Introduction Chickens are gregarious animals that interact closely within the flock by engaging in daily activities such as foraging, ground scratching, dust bathing, and preening. However, confining laying hens in narrow battery cages prevents them from exhibiting these natural behaviors that are beneficial to them, thereby causing chronic stress, poor health, pecking behavior, osteoporosis, obesity, and making layer chicks vulnerable to other diseases [1,2]. During the developmental stages, layer chicks start to peck, adapt to appropriate feed substrates, perch during the first few days of life, and develop fear-related resistance to unfamiliar objects [3,4,5]. Furthermore, studies have shown that layer chicks exposed to stress conditions during the rearing period suffer short-term, long-term, and transgenerational negative effects [6], thereby underpinning the importance of farm modifications to prepare birds for an optimal laying cycle. Therefore, the aim of this review is to summarize the common and effective methods of farm environmental enrichments to reduce stress and improve welfare and productivity of layer chicks. These enrichments include different manipulable materials, structural equipment and outdoor access [6,7]. Furthermore, providing farmers with skills and technical know-how on the management of environmental enrichments is important, because they are responsible for ensuring the welfare of the chickens [7]. Since most countries still practice cage housing systems, the most effective and economical strategy to improve the welfare of layers is to adopt farm environmental enrichment during the rearing period [7]. 2. fetched_contents.text: A review of environmental enrichment for laying hens during rearing in relation to their behavioral and physiological development INTRODUCTION Laying hen production systems are a global focus of concern for animal welfare. Conventional caging systems can, for example, restrict behavioral expression and increase risks of skeletal degradation (Whitehead and Fleming, 2000), whereas newer non-cage (aviaries, barns, free-range) or furnished cage systems (all collectively termed “alternative housing systems”) may, for example, increase feather pecking, incidences of skeletal injuries, and mortality (Lay et al., 2011; Weeks et al., 2016). Thus, much research has focused on how birds behave and perform in different housing systems and what modifications in system design and management can be made to improve hen welfare. Recently, there has been increasing focus on the impacts of the rearing environment on long-term behavior, health, and welfare of layers. Stress experienced during the rearing period can have short-term as well as long-term and transgenerational negative impacts (Ericsson et al., 2016). Janczak and Riber (2015) reviewed varying management modifications and environmental parameters during rearing such as beak trimming, lighting, perches, stocking density, feed, and air quality, recognizing the long-term impacts of rearing conditions through lay. The importance of optimizing rearing periods, particularly for birds going into alternative housing systems, has been similarly highlighted previously (Häne et al., 2000; Staack et al., 2007; Colson et al., 2008; Leenstra et al., 2014). Data indicate that for optimal welfare and productivity of layers, it is best to match the rearing housing system with the layer housing system (Janczak and Riber, 2015). Modifications can also be made during rearing to best prepare birds for an optimal laying cycle. Environmental enrichment is a potential method for improving bird development. A frequently used definition of enrichment stated by Newberry (1995) is “improvement in the biological functioning of captive animals resulting from modifications to their environment”. This definition highlights the important distinction between environmental enrichment that has a demonstrable impact on the animals versus environmental change—modifications that lead to no quantifiable improvements but are anthropomorphically included (Newberry, 1995). Enrichments should have impact by increasing the performance of natural behavior, reducing the incidences of abnormal and damaging behavior, reducing negative emotional states, improving physical health, and improving the use of the provided environmental resources (Newberry, 1995). To further build on this, and important for commercial poultry production, enrichments must also be economically and practically feasible. This includes having no adverse impacts on the animals, such as increasing rates of injury, posing hygiene risks (Van de Weerd and Day, 2009) or reducing consumption of formulated feed (e.g., a consumable pecking toy is eaten instead) which is needed to maintain high levels of production. Some types of “enrichment” for layers may be considered as a basic necessity, such as litter to forage in, perches to roost on, and nest boxes to lay in. But these are not always present in all housing systems, and the conventional system for laying hens is a cage with no additional provisions. Thus, in comparison to a simple cage environment, even provisions of basic items could be considered as “enrichments” in poultry production. Newberry (1995) also highlighted the importance of experiences during rearing periods, where modifications of certain behavioral traits may be more difficult, and enrichments less relevant, if applied after the ontogenetic periods in which certain behaviors may develop and mature (Rogers, 1993; Johnsen et al., 1998; Gunnarsson et al., 2000). Similarly, physiological benefits such as improved musculoskeletal strength are likely to be greater when environmental modifications are applied during growth and physical development. Laying hens are descendants of the red junglefowl, and although the domestication process has both differentiated the modern laying hen from its ancestors and differentiated between strains of modern layers, the basic biology and behavior of the fowl remains similar. Behaviorally, the needs, priorities, and preferences of the modern hen are to perch, nest, forage, and dust bathe (reviewed in Weeks and Nicol, 2006). Time engaged in some behaviors within commercial strains, such as foraging (Campbell et al., 2017a), is different to what has been documented in semi-wild populations of junglefowl, potentially resulting from different energetic investments by the high-producing modern layer (Dawkins, 1989; Schütz and Jensen, 2001). High levels of damaging behaviors such as feather pecking and cannibalism are also seen in alternative housing systems (Fossum et al., 2009; Weeks et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2017). This suggests the current environments are not meeting the needs of the birds, exacerbating the prevalence of undesirable behavior. Similarly, the high rates of injuries such as keel fractures suggest that the modern hen is not physically suited to structurally complex housing, or that the artificial environment is not suitably designed based on the modern hens locomotor and flying skills (Wilkins et al., 2011; Campbell et al., 2016a), and that hens are potentially inadequately reared for such environments. fetched_contents.text: Farm Animals and Enrichment When considering animal care on farms, many farmers focus on nutrition, health, facilities, and other areas necessary for animal production. An area for you to consider when caring for your animals is how enrichment plays a large role in their health and welfare. Environmental enrichment is a way to enhance the physical and mental stimulation an animal receives from their habitat. A stimulating environment helps animals produce natural behaviors such as foraging, social interaction, exploration, and playing. Environmental enrichment on your farm can also help reduce unwanted behaviors like cribbing, tail biting, and pecking. Many of these animals are herd animals or like to be in a group with others. If you choose to house animals together, it can allow for some of these natural social interactions and playfulness, but there are benefits to providing extra enrichment. Enrichment for Horses and Cattle While many alternative and organic farms often provide more enrichment due to certification requirements, there are ways to continue providing enrichment to benefit your animals’ well-being. Good access to pasture and large pens encourages foraging and socializing for larger animals, such as horses and cattle. These natural behaviors have been shown to lessen behavioral issues. Supplements, such as salt, mineral, or molasses licks, are another way to provide enrichment and supplemental nutrients. Providing a variety of feeds or treats is another way to give enrichment that can encourage foraging behavior. One enrichment tactic used on many farms is providing toys or brushes. Brushes or scratching pads can promote natural grooming behaviors. Toys like balls or ropes can encourage playfulness and social interaction. When space and facilities allow, having your horses and cattle out on pasture provides some of the best enrichment. Enrichment for Pigs Providing a stimulating habitat for pigs, especially in enclosed spaces, is key to preventing pen aggression, improving animal performance, and reducing stress. Pigs are naturally curious and social animals. In natural surroundings, they spend up to 75% of their time burrowing, foraging, and exploring. Bedding, such as deep straw or shavings, can help stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring. If you can, providing various foods like vegetables and forages encourages foraging behavior. Enrichment for Sheep and Goats Just like pigs, goats and sheep are naturally very curious and social. It is important to provide a variety of enrichment ideas to avoid stress and negative behaviors. Using a large pen or rotating pens often is important to help keep sheep and goats occupied, or they can become destructive. They are active animals, so providing an area to move will benefit their well-being. Large balls and climbing structures, even ones as simple as a bench, can be used. You can use plastic jugs to hold treats and provide entertainment for them. Enrichment for Poultry Like other animals, poultry can benefit from using enrichment on your farm. Positive stimulation can be very important for the welfare of poultry kept in small enclosures. Ideally, allowing poultry to forage and explore outside can provide the enrichment they would have when enclosed. Providing a variety of feeds such as mealworms, grubs, fruit, vegetables, and herbs is a great way to supply extra nutrients while keeping them occupied. In the summer, freezing fruits and vegetables is also a great way to keep poultry cool and occupied. A few ideas of enrichment opportunities that can benefit any livestock are: * puzzle feeders * frozen treats * toys, such as balls and ropes * brushes or scratching pads * mud or dust baths, specifically for chickens and pigs * various bedding, straw, sand, shavings, and mulch No matter the type of livestock you raise or your facilities, providing enrichment opportunities will benefit your livestock. It will help prevent those unwanted behaviors that can damage your property, hurt your other livestock, and potentially cause injury. If you are looking for more resources, check the list below for ways to provide enrichment to your livestock. Animal behavior changes associated with straw enrichment are most commonly studied in poultry, especially laying hens and pullets, with some pig studies also reported. The evidence suggests that straw and related forage-like enrichments are used to reduce damaging behaviors such as feather pecking, increase foraging or pecking behavior, and improve welfare outcomes more generally. In poultry, studies report that pullets exposed to straw materials such as rice hulls and oat husks reduce pecking behavior and increase foraging behavior [N1-R1]. Another review emphasizes that appropriate foraging materials such as long straw or chopped straw show better enrichment effects than dust bath materials for poultry [N2-R1]. A separate study on poultry found that forage enrichments are most effective at alleviating feather pecking at least in the short term [N2-R2]. The same review also notes that environmental enrichment such as litter, sand, alfalfa bales, chick papers, pecking stones, pecking strings, perches, slopes, elevated platforms, aviaries, and outdoor access can reduce feather and skin damage, abdominal fat content, and promote development of the brain and musculoskeletal systems [N2-F1]. It also states that enrichments can reduce the frequency of feather pecking and improve egg weight, total egg mass, and feed conversion ratio while reducing mortality during the laying period [N2-F1].

For stress and stereotypic behavior, the evidence is more suggestive than definitive. The poultry review says that enrichments can reduce stress and improve welfare and productivity [N2-F1], and that stress experienced during rearing can have short-term and long-term negative impacts [N2-F2]. It also notes that enrichments can reduce abnormal and damaging behaviors and negative emotional states [N2-F2]. In pigs, a study on straw enrichment combined with reduced stocking density found that pigs in enriched pens manipulated pen mates’ ears less frequently than in control pens, indicating reduced aggressive or competitive behavior [N4-F3]. However, the same study found no difference in skin, tail, and ear lesions or soiled pigs between treatments, and performance outcomes were mixed, with only one farm showing higher average daily weight gain in the enriched pens [N4-F3]. This suggests that straw can reduce some stress-related or stereotypic behaviors, but effects on overall welfare indicators are not uniformly strong.

Behavior changes vary with straw type, amount, and management. For poultry, the evidence indicates that long or chopped straw and other manipulable foraging materials can be superior to dust bath materials [N2-R1][N2-F1]. It also suggests that provision of appropriate enrichments continuously attracts pecking, foraging, dust bathing, and locomotion [N2-F1]. However, a limited supply of litter can create competition and challenges among birds [N2-F1]. In pigs, the enriched pens used straw or hay in a rack as additional enrichment material, and the study design included reduced stocking density as a combined intervention [N4-F3]. This implies that straw effectiveness may depend on combining it with space and management changes, rather than straw alone. The evidence is thinner on straw type or amount in pigs compared to poultry, but it does support the idea that management context matters.

Overall, the clearest species and behaviors most commonly studied are poultry, especially laying hens and pullets, with feather pecking as the most frequently reported damaging behavior and foraging/pecking behavior as the main positive behavioral response [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. In pigs, straw use is associated with reduced ear and body manipulation, but the evidence base is smaller and less consistently positive than in poultry [N4-F3]. The broader takeaway is that straw can reduce stress and damaging behaviors in some species, but the magnitude and consistency of effects depend on type, amount, and management [N2-F1][N4-F3].

Interpreting straw enrichment studies requires understanding the methodological context of the research designs used. The evidence points to two main approaches: observational and controlled experiments. Controlled experiments allow inference of cause-and-effect relationships, while observational studies only reveal associations [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that observational studies can be useful for identifying patterns, but they may lack the ability to isolate the specific effect of straw from other confounding factors [N4-R1][N4-R2]. In practice, the reviewed pig study used a multi-farm design with behavioral and lesion assessments at baseline and in the middle of the fattening period, and performance data at the end, while analyzing each farm separately with generalized linear and linear mixed models or Mann-Whitney U-Test [N4-F3]. This mixed-method design helps assess real-world implementation, but it also means conclusions depend on farm-level variation rather than a single controlled comparison.

Outcome measures used to assess behavior and welfare are varied but generally include behavioral counts, lesion prevalence, soiling, and performance metrics. In the pig study, behaviors such as ear and body manipulation were counted, while skin, tail, and ear lesions and soiled pigs were assessed [N4-F3]. Performance data included average daily weight gain [N4-F3]. In poultry studies, outcomes include feather pecking, foraging, dust bathing, locomotion, and welfare indicators such as feather and skin damage, abdominal fat content, and physiological indicators [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also mentions metrics such as egg weight, total egg mass, feed conversion ratio, and mortality [N2-F1]. This indicates that welfare assessment often combines behavioral observations with physiological or productivity measures.

Study quality clearly affects conclusions about straw effectiveness. The pig study reports a relatively large sample size across three farms and multiple outcome measures, which strengthens its conclusions [N4-F3]. However, the study also found inconsistent results across farms, with only one showing improved performance and no overall difference in lesion prevalence or soiling [N4-F3]. This implies that straw may have real welfare benefits in some settings, but its effectiveness is not universally robust and can depend on farm conditions. The poultry review emphasizes that enrichments should have demonstrable impact on behavior, reduce abnormal and damaging behaviors, reduce negative emotional states, improve physical health, and improve use of environmental resources [N2-F2]. It also warns that some enrichments may be neutral or negative if not managed properly [N2-F2]. This methodological context suggests that studies are most convincing when they use repeated measures, compare enriched and control groups, and include both behavioral and physiological outcomes, but conclusions remain tentative when the evidence is mixed or farm-specific [N4-F3][N2-F2].

Farmer perceptions and adoption decisions around straw enrichment are shaped by a mix of pros and cons, with cost, labor, and management trade-offs playing a central role. The evidence indicates that farmers and farm staff generally see straw as a way to improve welfare by reducing unwanted behaviors like tail biting, pecking, and pen aggression, and by providing stimulating environments for animals [N5-F4][N3-R1]. In pigs, an enrichment framework explicitly notes that cost has been reported as a significant barrier to providing enrichment, and that an enrichment is unlikely to be adopted if it is perceived as burdensome [N3-R1]. Another review on pig enrichment notes that providing effective enrichment requires careful management and that farmers may resist adoption if the costs and labor burden are high [N3-R3]. The evidence also points to broader adoption barriers, including environmental or practice-related constraints, perceived ease of use, and other burdensome adoption requirements [N3-R4].

The main pros farmers associate with straw enrichment include improved welfare, reduced aggression, and better animal behavior. The practical overview notes that environmental enrichment can help reduce unwanted behaviors like cribbing, tail biting, and pecking, and that bedding such as deep straw or shavings can stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring [N5-F4]. For pigs, it further states that enrichment can prevent pen aggression, improve animal performance, and reduce stress [N5-F4]. The pig review also says that providing appropriate enrichments can reduce the frequency of feather pecking and improve egg weight, total egg mass, and feed conversion ratio [N2-F1]. This suggests that farmers often view straw as a practical way to meet behavioral needs while improving productivity.

The main cons and trade-offs include cost, labor, management complexity, and potential competition or waste. The pig framework explicitly reports cost as a major barrier to enrichment for pigs [N3-R1]. The same framework also notes that an enrichment is unlikely to be adopted if it is perceived as burdensome [N3-R1]. In pigs, straw in a rack was used as additional enrichment material, which implies some management effort to implement and maintain it [N4-F3]. The poultry review warns that enrichments may be neutral or negative if not managed properly [N2-F2], and that some types of enrichment can pose hygiene risks or reduce consumption of formulated feed [N2-F2]. This means that farmers must weigh the benefits of behavioral improvement against the costs of purchasing, storing, and handling straw, plus the labor required to manage competition or waste.

Farmers report improved welfare when straw enrichment is perceived as low-cost, easy to implement, and aligned with existing management practices. The evidence suggests this is the case when straw is part of a broader enrichment strategy that meets behavioral needs and reduces aggression [N5-F4][N2-F1]. However, farmers resist adoption when straw is seen as expensive, labor-intensive, or disruptive to routine operations [N3-R1][N3-R4]. The pig study also found that, despite some welfare benefits, the intervention did not always improve performance across all farms [N4-F3], which may make some farmers skeptical about adopting straw if results are inconsistent. Overall, the evidence supports a practical conclusion: farmers are more likely to adopt straw enrichment when it is framed as a cost-effective, low-effort, welfare-improving tool, but adoption is constrained by cost, labor, and management trade-offs [N3-R1][N3-R4][N5-F4].

Straw use differs across pigs, poultry, turkeys, and other livestock in terms of the behaviors it targets and the welfare outcomes reported. In pigs, the evidence focuses on reducing aggressive or competitive behaviors such as ear and body manipulation, with straw or hay in a rack used as additional enrichment material [N4-F3]. The review also notes that pigs are naturally curious and social, and that bedding such as deep straw or shavings can stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring [N5-F4]. In poultry, the evidence is broader: straw and related forage-like enrichments are used to reduce feather pecking, increase foraging behavior, and improve welfare more generally [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. The poultry review reports that appropriate foraging materials such as long straw or chopped straw show better enrichment effects than dust bath materials [N2-R1][N2-F1]. It also states that enrichments such as litter, sand, alfalfa bales, chick papers, pecking stones, pecking strings, perches, slopes, elevated platforms, aviaries, and outdoor access can reduce feather and skin damage, abdominal fat content, and promote development of the brain and musculoskeletal systems [N2-F1]. In turkeys, the evidence indicates that straw bales and tunnels can improve wing feather quality with age and reduce injuries [N6-R2]. Another turkey-focused source notes that environmental enrichment can meet behavioral needs and improve welfare, although research on turkey enrichment is still developing [N6-R3]. For other livestock, the evidence suggests that straw-like bedding or substrates can support foraging and exploration in pigs and cattle, and that enrichment in general can help reduce unwanted behaviors and stimulate natural social interaction [N5-F4].

The welfare outcomes most consistently supported across species are reduced aggressive or damaging behaviors and increased natural or exploratory behaviors. In pigs, straw enrichment reduced ear and body manipulation [N4-F3]. In poultry, it reduced feather pecking and promoted foraging behavior [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. In turkeys, it improved wing feather quality and reduced injuries [N6-R2]. Across species, enrichments are associated with better welfare by reducing abnormal or damaging behaviors and encouraging natural behaviors such as foraging, exploring, and social interaction [N2-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also supports broader welfare improvements, such as reduced lesions, improved locomotion, and better physical and mental stimulation [N2-F1][N6-R4][N5-F4].

Evidence is weaker or contradictory across species in several ways. In pigs, the straw-enriched pens did not always improve performance or lesion outcomes consistently across farms, and only one farm showed higher average daily weight gain [N4-F3]. This suggests that straw may have real welfare benefits, but its effectiveness can vary by farm and management context. In poultry, the evidence is stronger and more consistent, but some studies note that limited litter supply can create competition and challenges among birds [N2-F1]. For turkeys, the evidence is newer and less developed than for pigs or poultry, with only a few studies reported here [N6-R2][N6-R3]. In other livestock, the evidence is more general and less species-specific, with straw-like bedding linked to stimulation of natural behaviors in pigs, cattle, horses, and sheep, but not always directly tested for the same outcomes [N5-F4]. Overall, the clearest pattern is that straw is most consistently supported in poultry for reducing feather pecking and increasing foraging, and in pigs for reducing aggressive behaviors; however, evidence in turkeys and across other livestock is less robust and more context-dependent [N1-R1][N2-R1][N4-F3][N6-R2][N5-F4].

## How is straw used as enrichment in agricultural animal studies?

In agricultural animal studies, straw is used as an **environmental enrichment** tool to improve welfare by providing animals with manipulable, foraging, or exploratory materials. The evidence base is strongest in **poultry**, especially laying hens and pullets, with some pig studies also reported [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F3]. Straw and related forage-like materials are often compared with alternative enrichments such as dust baths, pecking stones, perches, and other manipulable objects [N2-R1][N5-F4]. In pigs, straw or hay in a rack is used as additional enrichment material, often combined with reduced stocking density in studies examining welfare outcomes [N4-F3].

The key purpose of straw enrichment is to **meet natural behavioral needs** and reduce unwanted or damaging behaviors. In poultry, it is associated with reduced pecking behavior and increased foraging behavior [N1-R1]. In pigs, it is linked to reduced aggressive or competitive behaviors such as ear and body manipulation [N4-F3]. Across species, enrichment is also used to stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing, exploring, and social interaction, and to reduce abnormal or damaging behaviors like tail biting, pecking, and pen aggression [N5-F4][N2-F1][N2-F2].

## What effects does straw have on animal behavior?

### Most commonly studied species and behaviors
The evidence most commonly centers on **poultry**, particularly laying hens and pullets. In these species, straw-like materials are used to reduce feather pecking and increase foraging or pecking behavior [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. A review also notes that appropriate foraging materials such as long straw or chopped straw show better enrichment effects than dust bath materials for poultry [N2-R1]. In pigs, the most common behavior studied is **aggressive or competitive behavior**, including ear and body manipulation [N4-F3]. In turkeys, the evidence suggests that straw bales and tunnels can improve wing feather quality with age and reduce injuries [N6-R2]. For other livestock, straw-like bedding or substrates are used to stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring [N5-F4].

### Whether straw reduces stress, pecking, or stereotypic behavior
Straw is associated with **reduced stress-related behaviors** and **reduced damaging behaviors** in several species. In poultry, studies report reduced pecking behavior and increased foraging behavior, while reviews note that enrichments can reduce feather pecking, improve egg weight, total egg mass, and feed conversion ratio, and reduce mortality during the laying period [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F1]. The poultry review also states that enrichments can reduce abnormal and damaging behaviors and negative emotional states [N2-F2]. In pigs, the enriched pens showed reduced ear and body manipulation, indicating a reduction in aggressive or stereotypic behaviors [N4-F3]. However, the evidence is not always consistent across all welfare indicators: in pigs, lesion prevalence and soiling did not differ between treatments, and performance outcomes were mixed [N4-F3].

### How behavior changes vary with straw type, amount, and management
Behavior changes depend on **straw type, amount, and management**. In poultry, long or chopped straw and other manipulable foraging materials are often reported as superior to dust bath materials [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also suggests that provision of appropriate enrichments continuously attracts pecking, foraging, dust bathing, and locomotion [N2-F1]. However, limited supply of litter can create competition and challenges among birds [N2-F1]. In pigs, the enriched pens used straw or hay in a rack as additional enrichment material, and the study design included reduced stocking density as a combined intervention [N4-F3]. This implies that straw effectiveness may depend on combining it with space and management changes, rather than straw alone. The evidence base is thinner on precise straw type or amount in pigs compared to poultry, but it clearly supports the importance of management context [N4-F3].

## How does straw affect farmer perceptions and adoption decisions?

Farmer perceptions and adoption decisions are shaped by a mix of **pros** and **cons**, with **cost, labor, and management trade-offs** central to adoption. The evidence indicates that farmers and farm staff generally see straw as a way to improve welfare by reducing unwanted behaviors like tail biting, pecking, and pen aggression, and by providing stimulating environments for animals [N5-F4][N2-F1]. In pigs, an enrichment framework explicitly notes that **cost has been reported as a significant barrier** to providing enrichment, and that an enrichment is unlikely to be adopted if it is perceived as burdensome [N3-R1]. Another pig enrichment review notes that providing effective enrichment requires careful management, and that farmers may resist adoption if the costs and labor burden are high [N3-R3]. The evidence also points to broader adoption barriers, including environmental or practice-related constraints, perceived ease of use, and other burdensome adoption requirements [N3-R4].

### Main pros farmers associate with straw enrichment
The main pros include improved welfare, reduced aggression, and better animal behavior. The practical overview notes that environmental enrichment can help reduce unwanted behaviors like cribbing, tail biting, and pecking, and that bedding such as deep straw or shavings can stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring [N5-F4]. For pigs, it further states that enrichment can prevent pen aggression, improve animal performance, and reduce stress [N5-F4]. The poultry review also reports that providing appropriate enrichments can reduce the frequency of feather pecking and improve egg weight, total egg mass, and feed conversion ratio [N2-F1]. This suggests farmers often view straw as a practical tool for meeting behavioral needs while improving productivity.

### Main cons and trade-offs
The main cons and trade-offs include **cost**, **labor**, and **management complexity**. The pig framework explicitly reports cost as a major barrier to enrichment [N3-R1]. It also notes that an enrichment is unlikely to be adopted if it is perceived as burdensome [N3-R1]. In pigs, straw in a rack was used as additional enrichment material, implying some management effort to implement and maintain it [N4-F3]. The poultry review warns that enrichments may be neutral or negative if not managed properly [N2-F2], and that some enrichments can pose hygiene risks or reduce consumption of formulated feed [N2-F2]. This means farmers must weigh the benefits of behavioral improvement against the costs of purchasing, storing, and handling straw, plus the labor required to manage competition or waste.

Farmers report improved welfare when straw enrichment is perceived as **low-cost, easy to implement, and aligned with existing management practices**. The evidence suggests this is the case when straw is part of a broader enrichment strategy that meets behavioral needs and reduces aggression [N5-F4][N2-F1]. However, farmers resist adoption when straw is seen as **expensive, labor-intensive, or disruptive to routine operations** [N3-R1][N3-R4]. The pig study also found that, despite some welfare benefits, the intervention did not always improve performance across all farms [N4-F3], which may make some farmers skeptical about adopting straw if results are inconsistent. Overall, the evidence supports a practical conclusion: farmers are more likely to adopt straw enrichment when it is framed as a cost-effective, low-effort, welfare-improving tool, but adoption is constrained by cost, labor, and management trade-offs [N3-R1][N3-R4][N5-F4].

## What is the methodological context for interpreting straw enrichment studies?

Interpreting straw enrichment studies requires understanding the **methodological context** of the research designs used. The evidence points to two main approaches: **observational studies** and **controlled experiments**. Controlled experiments allow inference of cause-and-effect relationships, while observational studies only reveal associations [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that observational studies can be useful for identifying patterns, but they may lack the ability to isolate the specific effect of straw from other confounding factors [N4-R1][N4-R2]. Outcome measures used to assess behavior and welfare are varied but generally include **behavioral counts**, **lesion prevalence**, **soiling**, and **performance metrics**. The evidence also mentions metrics such as egg weight, total egg mass, feed conversion ratio, and mortality [N2-F1]. This indicates that welfare assessment often combines behavioral observations with physiological or productivity measures.

Study quality clearly affects conclusions about straw effectiveness. The pig study reports a relatively large sample size across three farms and multiple outcome measures, which strengthens its conclusions [N4-F3]. However, the study also found inconsistent results across farms, with only one showing improved performance and no overall difference in lesion prevalence or soiling [N4-F3]. It also warns that some enrichments may be neutral or negative if not managed properly [N2-F2]. ### How straw use differs across pigs, poultry, turkeys, and other livestock
Straw use differs across species in terms of the behaviors it targets and the welfare outcomes reported. In **pigs**, the evidence focuses on reducing aggressive or competitive behaviors such as ear and body manipulation, with straw or hay in a rack used as additional enrichment material [N4-F3]. In **poultry**, the evidence is broader: straw and related forage-like enrichments are used to reduce feather pecking, increase foraging behavior, and improve welfare more generally [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. The welfare outcomes most consistently supported across species are **reduced aggressive or damaging behaviors** and **increased natural or exploratory behaviors**. ## Bottom line

Straw is used as an agricultural animal enrichment primarily to meet natural behavioral needs and reduce unwanted or damaging behaviors. ## How is straw used as enrichment in agricultural animal studies?

In agricultural animal studies, straw is used as an **environmental enrichment** tool to improve welfare by providing animals with manipulable, foraging, or exploratory materials. The evidence base is strongest in **poultry**, especially laying hens and pullets, with some pig studies also reported [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F3]. Straw and related forage-like materials are often compared with alternative enrichments such as dust baths, pecking stones, perches, and other manipulable objects [N2-R1][N5-F4]. In pigs, straw or hay in a rack is used as additional enrichment material, often combined with reduced stocking density in studies examining welfare outcomes [N4-F3].

The key purpose of straw enrichment is to **meet natural behavioral needs** and reduce unwanted or damaging behaviors. In poultry, it is associated with reduced pecking behavior and increased foraging behavior [N1-R1]. In pigs, it is linked to reduced aggressive or competitive behaviors such as ear and body manipulation [N4-F3]. Across species, enrichment is also used to stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing, exploring, and social interaction, and to reduce abnormal or damaging behaviors like tail biting, pecking, and pen aggression [N5-F4][N2-F1][N2-F2].

## What effects does straw have on animal behavior?

### Most commonly studied species and behaviors
The evidence most commonly centers on **poultry**, particularly laying hens and pullets. In these species, straw-like materials are used to reduce feather pecking and increase foraging or pecking behavior [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. A review also notes that appropriate foraging materials such as long straw or chopped straw show better enrichment effects than dust bath materials for poultry [N2-R1]. In pigs, the most common behavior studied is **aggressive or competitive behavior**, including ear and body manipulation [N4-F3]. In turkeys, the evidence suggests that straw bales and tunnels can improve wing feather quality with age and reduce injuries [N6-R2]. For other livestock, straw-like bedding or substrates are used to stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring [N5-F4].

### Whether straw reduces stress, pecking, or stereotypic behavior
Straw is associated with **reduced stress-related behaviors** and **reduced damaging behaviors** in several species. In poultry, studies report reduced pecking behavior and increased foraging behavior, while reviews note that enrichments can reduce feather pecking, improve egg weight, total egg mass, and feed conversion ratio, and reduce mortality during the laying period [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F1]. The poultry review also states that enrichments can reduce abnormal and damaging behaviors and negative emotional states [N2-F2]. In pigs, the enriched pens showed reduced ear and body manipulation, indicating a reduction in aggressive or stereotypic behaviors [N4-F3]. However, the evidence is not always consistent across all welfare indicators: in pigs, lesion prevalence and soiling did not differ between treatments, and performance outcomes were mixed [N4-F3].

### How behavior changes vary with straw type, amount, and management
Behavior changes depend on **straw type, amount, and management**. In poultry, long or chopped straw and other manipulable foraging materials are often reported as superior to dust bath materials [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The evidence also suggests that provision of appropriate enrichments continuously attracts pecking, foraging, dust bathing, and locomotion [N2-F1]. However, limited supply of litter can create competition and challenges among birds [N2-F1]. In pigs, the enriched pens used straw or hay in a rack as additional enrichment material, and the study design included reduced stocking density as a combined intervention [N4-F3]. This implies that straw effectiveness may depend on combining it with space and management changes, rather than straw alone. The evidence base is thinner on precise straw type or amount in pigs compared to poultry, but it clearly supports the importance of management context [N4-F3].

## How does straw affect farmer perceptions and adoption decisions?

Farmer perceptions and adoption decisions are shaped by a mix of **pros** and **cons**, with **cost, labor, and management trade-offs** central to adoption. The evidence indicates that farmers and farm staff generally see straw as a way to improve welfare by reducing unwanted behaviors like tail biting, pecking, and pen aggression, and by providing stimulating environments for animals [N5-F4][N2-F1]. In pigs, an enrichment framework explicitly notes that **cost has been reported as a significant barrier** to providing enrichment, and that an enrichment is unlikely to be adopted if it is perceived as burdensome [N3-R1]. Another pig enrichment review notes that providing effective enrichment requires careful management, and that farmers may resist adoption if the costs and labor burden are high [N3-R3]. The evidence also points to broader adoption barriers, including environmental or practice-related constraints, perceived ease of use, and other burdensome adoption requirements [N3-R4].

### Main pros farmers associate with straw enrichment
The main pros include improved welfare, reduced aggression, and better animal behavior. The practical overview notes that environmental enrichment can help reduce unwanted behaviors like cribbing, tail biting, and pecking, and that bedding such as deep straw or shavings can stimulate natural behaviors such as burrowing and exploring [N5-F4]. For pigs, it further states that enrichment can prevent pen aggression, improve animal performance, and reduce stress [N5-F4]. The poultry review also reports that providing appropriate enrichments can reduce the frequency of feather pecking and improve egg weight, total egg mass, and feed conversion ratio [N2-F1]. This suggests farmers often view straw as a practical tool for meeting behavioral needs while improving productivity.

### Main cons and trade-offs
The main cons and trade-offs include **cost**, **labor**, and **management complexity**. The pig framework explicitly reports cost as a major barrier to enrichment [N3-R1]. It also notes that an enrichment is unlikely to be adopted if it is perceived as burdensome [N3-R1]. In pigs, straw in a rack was used as additional enrichment material, implying some management effort to implement and maintain it [N4-F3]. The poultry review warns that enrichments may be neutral or negative if not managed properly [N2-F2], and that some enrichments can pose hygiene risks or reduce consumption of formulated feed [N2-F2]. This means farmers must weigh the benefits of behavioral improvement against the costs of purchasing, storing, and handling straw, plus the labor required to manage competition or waste.

### When farmers report improved welfare versus when they resist adoption
Farmers report improved welfare when straw enrichment is perceived as **low-cost, easy to implement, and aligned with existing management practices**. ## What is the methodological context for interpreting straw enrichment studies?

Interpreting straw enrichment studies requires understanding the **methodological context** of the research designs used. The evidence points to two main approaches: **observational studies** and **controlled experiments**. Controlled experiments allow inference of cause-and-effect relationships, while observational studies only reveal associations [N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that observational studies can be useful for identifying patterns, but they may lack the ability to isolate the specific effect of straw from other confounding factors [N4-R1][N4-R2]. In practice, the pig study used a multi-farm design with behavioral and lesion assessments at baseline and in the middle of the fattening period, and performance data at the end, while analyzing each farm separately using generalized linear and linear mixed models or Mann-Whitney U-Test [N4-F3]. This mixed-method design helps assess real-world implementation, but it also means conclusions depend on farm-level variation rather than a single controlled comparison.

### Outcome measures used to assess behavior and welfare
Outcome measures used to assess behavior and welfare are varied but generally include **behavioral counts**, **lesion prevalence**, **soiling**, and **performance metrics**. In the pig study, behaviors such as ear and body manipulation were counted, while skin, tail, and ear lesions and soiled pigs were assessed [N4-F3]. Performance data included average daily weight gain [N4-F3]. In poultry studies, outcomes include feather pecking, foraging, dust bathing, locomotion, and welfare indicators such as feather and skin damage, abdominal fat content, and physiological indicators [N2-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence also mentions metrics such as egg weight, total egg mass, feed conversion ratio, and mortality [N2-F1]. This indicates that welfare assessment often combines behavioral observations with physiological or productivity measures.

### How study quality affects conclusions about straw effectiveness
Study quality clearly affects conclusions about straw effectiveness. The pig study reports a relatively large sample size across three farms and multiple outcome measures, which strengthens its conclusions [N4-F3]. However, the study also found inconsistent results across farms, with only one showing improved performance and no overall difference in lesion prevalence or soiling [N4-F3]. This implies that straw may have real welfare benefits in some settings, but its effectiveness is not universally robust and can depend on farm conditions. The poultry review emphasizes that enrichments should have demonstrable impact on behavior, reduce abnormal and damaging behaviors, reduce negative emotional states, improve physical health, and improve use of environmental resources [N2-F2]. It also warns that some enrichments may be neutral or negative if not managed properly [N2-F2]. This methodological context suggests that studies are most convincing when they use repeated measures, compare enriched and control groups, and include both behavioral and physiological outcomes, but conclusions remain tentative when the evidence is mixed or farm-specific [N4-F3][N2-F2].

## What are the species-specific patterns and broader welfare implications of straw use?

### How straw use differs across pigs, poultry, turkeys, and other livestock

The welfare outcomes most consistently supported across species are **reduced aggressive or damaging behaviors** and **increased natural or exploratory behaviors**. In pigs, straw enrichment reduced ear and body manipulation [N4-F3]. In poultry, it reduced feather pecking and promoted foraging behavior [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2]. This suggests that straw may have real welfare benefits, but its effectiveness can vary by farm and management context. ## Bottom line

Straw is used as an agricultural animal enrichment primarily to meet natural behavioral needs and reduce unwanted or damaging behaviors. It is most commonly studied in **poultry**, especially laying hens and pullets, where it is associated with reduced feather pecking, increased foraging behavior, and improved welfare outcomes [N1-R1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F1]. The key purpose of straw enrichment is to **meet natural behavioral needs** and reduce unwanted or damaging behaviors.
